result.summary: Hesiod advises his brother Perses on honest wealth, piety, and dealing with neighbours, friends and family. He then turns to farming: when to harvest and plough by the Pleiades, and how to prepare timber, ploughs, oxen and a ploughman in autumn.

scenes.title: Honest wealth and fear of Zeus
scenes.summary: Wealth taken by force or trickery is soon lost, and Zeus punishes wrongs against suppliants, guests, kin and parents. Perses is told to sacrifice purely to the gods.
scenes.stakes: Perses risks the gods' anger and the ruin of his house if he seeks wealth by wrongdoing.

scenes.title: Neighbours, giving and thrift
scenes.summary: Hesiod gives maxims on neighbours, fair measure, reciprocity, saving, wages and distrust of flattering women.
scenes.stakes: Carelessness in dealing with others brings loss, shame and want.

scenes.title: Work, seasons and Perses' debts
scenes.summary: Hesiod advises on household size, then on harvest and ploughing by the Pleiades. He scolds Perses for begging and tells him to prepare his house and not delay.
scenes.stakes: Perses faces hunger, debt and no help from neighbours if he does not work.

scenes.title: Autumn timber and the plough
scenes.summary: After the autumn rains Hesiod tells how to cut timber for mortar, axle, wheel and plough, and how to choose oxen and a ploughman.
scenes.stakes: Poor tools or unfit workers would break the plough and waste the sowing season.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable personification of generosity and greed as Give and Take.
Witty proverb about the value of good neighbours.
Classic advice on small, steady accumulation.

analysis.text: The passage joins morality and practical economy: honest dealing, reciprocity and diligent work are what the gods reward.
It reflects the life of small farmers in archaic Boeotia, who relied on neighbours, kin and seasonal timing, and its tone suits Hesiod's dispute with Perses.

legacy.text: Works and Days began the Greek tradition of didactic farming poetry, later echoed in Virgil's Georgics.

fun_facts.text: The numbered notes in the text are the translator's footnotes, explaining terms such as the Pleiades' rising and the farm tools.

language_notes.text: "Steal it through his tongue" means gain wealth by lying, flattery or persuasive deceit rather than by open force.
"Requittal" means repayment or retribution; here, divine punishment matching the wrong done.
"Goes up to his brother's bed" is a euphemism for adultery with a brother's wife.
"Propitiate" means to win the favour of the gods and turn away their anger.
"Come ungirt" means neighbours rush out at once without fastening their robes, while kinsmen stop to dress properly.
Meaning: a bad neighbour may cause or fail to prevent the loss of even a valuable ox, through theft or neglect.
"Lees" are the dregs or sediment at the bottom of a cask of wine.
"Cozen" means to cheat by coaxing or flattery.
'You should die old' means you should live to old age before dying, leaving one heir so the estate is not divided.
The Pleiades are a star cluster, said to be daughters of Atlas. Their rising in May and setting in November marked harvest and ploughing.
The Pleiades vanish from the night sky for about forty days in spring, then reappear; that is the time to sharpen the sickle.
'Strip to sow' means work without heavy clothing, stripped for labour, whatever the season's heat or effort demands.
'Demeter's fruits' means grain; Demeter is the goddess of cereal crops.
'Word-play' means clever arguments or talk, here Perses' empty pleading that will not feed him.
The slave woman is to follow the oxen as a farmhand, not be a wife; Hesiod prefers one who works the plough.
'At hand-grips with ruin' means constantly wrestling with disaster.
Sirius, the Dog Star, rises with summer heat; by autumn it is visible only briefly at night's start, so the scorching season is over.
A beetle here means a heavy mallet or wooden hammer, not an insect.
A felloe is a curved section of a wheel's rim; spans and palms are hand-based measures of length.
"Athena's handmen" means carpenters, craftsmen under the patronage of Athena, goddess of skills. The plough-tree is the main frame beam of the plough.
"All of a piece" means a plough made from one naturally bent timber; "jointed" means assembled from separate parts.
"Gaping after his fellows" means staring around at companions, being distracted from the work.

context_notes.text: Suppliants, guests and orphans were under Zeus's special protection; harming them or one's parents was a grave offence against divine order.
Libations were offerings of wine or other liquid poured out for the gods; incense and burnt meat were also standard offerings.
Hesiod's advice assumes a small farming community, where wages and loans were agreed by word and witness, not written contract.
Zeus is the chief god, giver of fortune; Hesiod admits he can bless a larger family, though he advises caution.
Perses is Hesiod's brother, who cheated him over their inheritance and now begs; this quarrel frames the whole poem.
Hesiod's farming advice follows natural signs, such as leaf-fall and the stars, rather than calendar dates.
Oxen were the main draught animals for ploughing in archaic Greece; Hesiod's advice stresses a pair at their peak of strength.

literary_notes.text: The balanced pairing of a bad neighbour as plague and a good one as blessing sharpens the contrast.
Giving and taking become two women, Give and Take, making the moral contrast vivid and memorable like a proverb.
Small additions build up to something great, a thrifty maxim that compresses a lesson on patience into one image.
The curt, closing generalisation about women reflects Hesiod's blunt, proverb-like didactic voice and his distrust of them.
'Work with work upon work' piles up the word to stress ceaseless labour.
Hesiod directly addresses Perses as 'Foolish', a scolding that makes the teaching personal.
Ruin is pictured as an opponent a lazy man grapples with, making procrastination a physical struggle.
"Almighty Zeus" and "men who are born to misery" frame the farmer's labour within divine power and human hardship.
The staid forty-year-old is contrasted with the restless young man, sketching the ideal worker through his steady temperament.
